summary:
Anterior, a clinician-led, Sequoia/NEA-backed company led by Anuj Iravane, builds AI agents for high-stakes healthcare administrative workflows (prior authorization, payment integrity, HEDIS). Their core task is policy-guided decision-making over highly unstructured faxed medical records — 300+ page scanned bundles representing a full clinical trajectory. In healthcare, where 95% accuracy is insufficient, this data is exactly what their evals need and exactly what contracts forbid them from retaining, reusing, deriving from, redacting, or anonymizing. Nothing survives into a persisted dataset.

Their answer is to synthetically generate the data by reversing the forward inference task. The forward task takes unstructured data plus a policy, follows a reasoning trace, and produces a label. Reversed, they sample a label, sample a trace, and build the record backward. Because Anterior models policies explicitly as symbolic decision trees, sampling traces is deterministic and uniform — a far better prior than asking an LLM to invent variety, which mode-collapses due to limited medical-record pre-training and helpfulness-biased objectives. This also exposes rare edge cases that production data rarely covers.

The LLM-based coarse-to-fine pipeline starts with patient invariants (sex, birth date, blood type), expands into an ordered patient journey of provider encounters, then fans out into per-encounter documents. A consistency eval catches contradictions across documents generated in parallel, and because generation starts from the label, a round-trip check guarantees correct labels by construction, eliminating ground truthing. All generation stays in text/markdown rather than rendered PDFs, since modern parsers convert back losslessly.

Critically, clinicians — not engineers — own the entire pipeline. It is modeled as a skills-based workflow on an internal generic agent harness, so adding a new document type for a new customer is a clinician-authored skill file with no engineering changes. Clinicians also steer generation in human-in-the-loop fashion, often pulling interesting production cases and generating look-alikes to model failure modes. As a result, ~90% of Anterior's datasets are now synthetic, clinicians separated synthetic from real only ~60% of the time in blind review, and most datasets are now built just-in-time for each customer deployment — simulating edge cases before going live rather than waiting for real customer data.

sections.title: Introduction and Anterior's problem space
sections.summary: Anuj Iravane introduces Anterior as a clinician-led, Sequoia/NEA-backed company running AI transformations for health plans. He frames the work as policy-guided decision-making over unstructured data and notes that ~70% of medical communication still moves by fax, producing 300+ page bundles full of handwriting, tables, and checkboxes. He stresses that 95% accuracy is not good enough in healthcare, yet contracts forbid retaining, reusing, deriving from, redacting, or anonymizing the PHI that their evals most need.

sections.title: The bet on synthetic generation
sections.summary: Anuj reframes the problem: when the dataset you most need is the one you cannot keep, generate it. Synthetic data is a hot topic across frontier labs, and LLMs are a promising tool, but one-shotting a 300-page record or asking a model to invent diverse clinical data causes mode collapse due to limited pre-training exposure and helpfulness-biased objectives.

sections.title: Reversing the forward task
sections.summary: The forward task takes unstructured data plus a policy, follows a reasoning trace, and arrives at a label. The team reverses it: sample a random label, derive a reasoning trace, then generate the record backward. The trick is having policies that can be sampled from deterministically.

sections.title: Policies as symbolic decision trees
sections.summary: Using a CPAP medical-necessity policy as an example, Anuj shows how policies enumerate conditions under which a device is approved or rejected. Anterior models policies explicitly as symbolic decision trees, which lets them deterministically sample diverse reasoning traces for any given outcome — a more uniform and effective prior than an LLM's free-form sampling. He notes this also exposes rare edge cases that customer samples miss, and references Cynthia's symbolic-causal-state approach as a peer.

sections.title: Coarse-to-fine synthetic record pipeline
sections.summary: Starting from a sampled label and trace as conditioning input, an LLM-based pipeline builds records layer by layer: patient invariants (sex, birth date, blood group) → an ordered patient journey of provider encounters → per-encounter document plans → fanned-out document generation. This keeps prompts token-efficient and scales to long journeys. A refinement loop runs an LLM-based consistency check across documents generated in parallel, catching contradictions.

sections.title: Round-trip check, text-only generation, and clinician ownership
sections.summary: Because generation starts from the label, a round-trip check guarantees the label matches the generated record, making labels correct by construction and skipping ground truthing. All generation stays in plain text/markdown rather than rendered PDFs, since state-of-the-art parsers convert PDFs back to markdown. The pipeline is largely LLM-based and easy to build, but Anuj flags the open question of who judges whether the synthetic records are any good — motivating clinician ownership of the pipeline.

sections.title: Clinicians as owners via skills on an agent harness
sections.summary: To answer who judges the data, Anterior empowers clinicians to own the whole pipeline in two ways: (1) human-in-the-loop steering at every generation step, where clinicians interject based on interesting production cases to produce look-alike records that model failure modes; and (2) modeling the entire pipeline as skills-based workflows on an internal generic agent harness, so adding a new customer-specific document type is a clinician-authored skill file with no engineering changes. Anuj argues skills are an amazing AI-engineer-to-domain-expert interface for vertical AI.

sections.title: Results and just-in-time datasets
sections.summary: Roughly 90% of Anterior's datasets are now synthetic, sustaining high production accuracy across deployments; blind-review clinician discrimination between synthetic and real is only ~60%. Most importantly, because data can be generated from scratch so quickly, most datasets are now built just-in-time for each customer deployment — letting Anterior model edge cases and test workflows before going live instead of waiting on customer data.

sections.title: Takeaways for building your own pipeline
sections.summary: Anuj distills recommendations for any domain: (1) try reversing the inference workflow; (2) sample diversity from an appropriate distribution for the use case; (3) emulate the process by which the data was actually generated (e.g., simulate patient encounters); and (4) give domain experts the keys, since they understand the data and drive recursive self-improvement — not AI engineers. He closes by noting the approach generalizes beyond healthcare, anywhere the data you need is ephemeral, sensitive, or expensive to label, so 'you won't be data poor.'

demonstrations: Worked example of a CPAP medical-necessity policy as a decision tree of approval/rejection conditions.

limitations: LLMs mode-collapse when asked to generate diverse, creative data in one shot.
Pre-training corpora have very little exposure to this medical-record data, hurting realism.
Pre/post-training objectives reward helpfulness over creativity and diversity.
Real-world contracts block even redacted/anonymized/derivative copies, leaving no persistent real dataset.
A 200-case customer eval at 95% does not cover rare edge cases outside that sample.
One-shotting a 300-page record with an LLM is impractical, mirroring the difficulty of one-shotting a novel.
Synthetic-vs-real fidelity is at ~60% clinician discrimination, described as 'room for improvement'.
